name: Wormwood (Artemisia absinthium)
short: Wormwood oil caused kidney failure (case report), seizures (19th-century studies). Thujone, in absinthe (a wormwood spirit), caused convulsions in animals. Crohn's trial: adverse events not reported.
text: A review of absinthe history describes thujone as a constituent of absinthe, a spirit containing wormwood; the cited abstracts do not state that wormwood herb or oil itself contains thujone. A toxicology review of thujone describes it as neurotoxic, causing excitation and convulsions in animal studies in a dose-dependent way, with uncertainty about the doses needed in humans and some equivocal evidence of cancer in rats; the review adds that the current view rather downgrades thujone's risk to humans, and that its breakdown by the liver enzymes CYP2A6 and CYP3A4 may give rise to potential metabolic interactions, without naming specific medicines. That absinthe history review also concludes that the only consistent conclusion from 19th-century studies is that wormwood oil, but not the absinthe drink, is a potent agent to cause seizures, and warns that uncontrolled trade in potentially unsafe herbal products such as absinthe essences sold online is a health risk; another review states that long-term use of wormwood essential oil may cause convulsions, sleeplessness and hallucinations. A published case report describes acute kidney failure caused by oil of wormwood bought over the internet; no abstract is available, so only its title is cited here. In a 10-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 40 patients with Crohn's disease, a herbal blend containing wormwood herb was taken while steroids were tapered; the abstract reports clinical results but does not report adverse events. No specific medicine interactions were named in the cited sources.
